Daveyton Turmoil

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The community of Daveyton is under siege by Nyaope gangs. Fed up with the lack of policing in their township they took the law into their hands with dire consequences.

Unique Selling Point:
A lack of police response to violence perpetrated in the Daveyton community, in the east rand of Johannesburg, has prompted residents to take revenge against the gang members by using vigilante township justice, with tyres and matchsticks in defense of their own peace and safety. The feeling is that the police have failed them.

Summary:
For some time now residents in Daveyton have been terrorized by thieves breaking into their homes. People are being killed in the streets by the gangs with little or no police intervention. In the past few weeks, violence escalated as the gangs went on a rampage. According Nonkululeko, a Daveyton resident, the gangs try and recruit young girls and boys and if they refuse they get necklaced. In the space of seven weeks 11 people have been killed.

On the 15th of August things got out of control, following the murder of two teenage girls by the gangs. The community turned vigilante and went in search of gang members. They say that some of the gang members attend the local school, Unity Secondary school and it was there that they took justice into their own hands by necklacing alleged gang members in front of children and staff. These gruesome visuals have been shared on social media.

Crime has always been an issue for the people of Daveyton, but with the emergence of gangs such as the “Freaks” and the “Avanzas” within the township the residents are afraid for their lives and those of their children and angry about a distinct lack of police protection. Finally, when they took matters into their own hands, the police reacted, patrolling the township trying to stop more bloodshed. This was only after the mob of residents necklaced the high school student suspected to be part of a gang. But the police themselves became perpetrators in the violence.


Further information:
In the aftermath of the violence Gauteng MEC Panyaza Lesufi along with Gauteng Community Safety MEC Sizakele Nkosi-Malobane visited the Unity Secondary school and the community to plead for calm and patience. MEC Nkosi Malobane says they have a couple of arrests and more will follow. Lesufi believes schools are a place of learning and gangterism should not interrupt the children’s learning.

According to Nonkululeko, while the police were patrolling the township, she and her cousin Petunia were standing outside their home when the police instructed them to go into the house. Nonkululeko says, she told them that they were not doing anything and were just standing there watching what was going on. When the police became aggressive, she and her cousin went into the house. While they were walking to the house one of the policemen put a rifle through the fence and shot at them three times with live ammunition. Petunia’s 15-year-old child was shot in the leg and as a result had to be sent to hospital. The cops that shot at them are believed to be from Benoni Police and when they called for assistance after the shooting it was Daveyton cops that arrived and told them to open a case against the Benoni police. Today, Pertunia’s child was sent back from hospital, with bullets still in her body and it’s alleged that the hospital told them the bullets will come out on their own.

A couple of students who have also been approached by the gangs to join them have come forward to Carte Blanche as they continue to worry about their safety. Not only are children in the community traumatized by the gangs but the actions of the community has had them fearing to go to school.

The residents of Daveyton live in fear and gangs are running rampant. Instead of the Police protecting them, there is more misery and brutality from the very same police. Cart Blanche investigates the turmoil.

Press Release:


In recent weeks, the streets Daveyton in Ekurhuleni have become shrouded in fear, after a sequence of deadly events. Gangsterism and gruesome killings paved the way, for a community to take justice into their own hands.


Script:


VO: East of Johannesburg lies Daveyton, by all appearances a normal town. But bubbling under the surface, gangsterism, drugs and gruesome murders are plaguing the community.

Douglas: you see here in Daveyton, There is a time bomb that keeps on ticking, tick tick.

VO: On the 15 Aug the time bomb exploded as some 500 residents took justice into their own hands, viciously beating one young man to death and another is still fighting for his life.

Nonkululeko: The community was very angry. That's when they started burning these small boys who are part of these gangs.

VO: And by Friday the 17th of August, as seen in this cell phone footage, they were still roaming the streets baying for blood and police were trying to disperse the crowds.//

Sound up of video through the window:

The streets are full of people
Like it’s so fucking full … hey guys I’m so scared

Cliffhanger

VO: So how did this town turn vigilante overnight?

Sound up of Daveyton community meeting..

Percy: We are sick and tired as citizens of Daveyton, of being ignored while we die.

Sound up: Now we are talking

VO: According to the community, Yende park and its surrounds have been the scene of three murders involving body mutilations over the last year, one as recently as July, and they feel the police are not doing enough. Residents and parents of the victims are desperate.

Father of murdered child: I'm one of the parents who lost a child here last year and my case just ended up in the air

Wandile's father: I am the father of Wandile who was recently killed and left here

Percy Dlamini: The crimes here at this very same park, people are being killed and being mutilated being left without their body parts. Women without breasts and men without their genitals.

We don’t have police… we’re on our own.

VO: Douglas Jobela, a concerned member of the Daveyton community, says the town has been terrorised by a number of gangs over the last three years.

Douglas: There’s the Freaks and the Avanzas. These gangsters became robbers. At the trains, robbing people on the streets and take their watches, phones, money, whatever. There are people who use school children to sell drugs for them.

Bongani: They wait at the gates and then when school's out they beat you up, You can be at your house, they accuse your parents to beat them up too

VO: Bongani, a school pupil in the area, whose identity we can’t reveal, knows the gangs very well. Children as young as 10 are being recruited.

Bongani: let's say they want you in the gang and then you don't want to be in a gang, they will beat you every day, just so that you can agree to join them.

But on the 15th of August, the tables had turned on the gangs and vigilantes were determined to root out the rot. Nonkululeko Mthunzi and her family who live in the area were directly affected by the mobs’ rage.

Nonkululeko: The time was about 8 pm. So my cousin comes to me and calls me and says, "There's a mob outside and they've mistaken my cousin for one of the boys that are part of the gangs." Luckily the neighbours could tell the people that, "No, this boy is not part of these gangs.

They had a list of these boys, where they lived. When they found one, they would ask him, "You must take out the other ones, or else we will burn you."

VO: Earlier that day, as seen in this cell phone footage, 18 year old school pupil Siyanda Mjoli, did not manage to escape. Nolwazi, Siyanda’s mother, was alerted by one of her neighbours that her son was being necklaced by a mob outside Unity School.

Nolwazi: So I left the house and ran there

Macfarlane: And when you got there?

Nolwazi: I got there he was lying on the ground already burned

LINK: This is the spot where the angry community brought Siyanda, asking him questions about being a member of a gang. There are still remnants of the tyre that was used to try and burn him alive.

Macfarlane: What kind of child is Siyanda Ma?

Nolwazi: He is alright.

Macfarlane: He doesn’t give you trouble?

Nolwazi: No. He once got into a fight with another boy and there was a case.

Macfarlane: So people here in Daveyton think that because of that now Siyanda is part of the gangsters.

Nolwazi: Yes, that's what they say. They say they can tell by the hats they wear - a wool hat with a pompom on top. They say if they have that hat and wear rings that means they are gangsters

Macfarlane: Did Siyanda wear those rings?

Nolwazi: Yes he did have those rings.

LINK: Siyanda is lying in this hospital. 80 percent of his body has been badly burnt. He's in severe pain and can barely move.//

VO: We were able to visit him in the isolation ward where he was still battling to breathe.

Macfarlane: Do you remember what happened on that day my brother?

Siyanda: When I think of it my heart gets painful. I don't even want to speak about it

VO: Siyanda hadn’t attended school that week. He was stopped by the mob whilst walking with a friend,// they accused him of being part of the Freaks gang

Siyanda: One took off my hat and said “the Freaks wear hats like this”. I told him my brother bought me the hat

VO: That’s when they attacked Siyanda, beat him, necklaced him with a tyre and lit it, but he managed to get away at first.

Siyanda: I got a chance to get into a container. I poured water over myself and it killed the fire.

VO: But Siyanda was recaptured and dragged to Unity Secondary School. The mob went on a rampage looking for more gang members, even assaulting the headmaster. When they couldn’t find any they burned Siyanda outside the school grounds.

Siyanda: They decided to use the tyre that
was already burning and they threw me onto it. That's when I took it and threw it back and then one of them hit me with a stick on the head. I couldn't see clearly, I just heard the police arrive. That's when they ran away.

VO: Since this violence, policing has been heightened in the area says SAPS Head of communication for Gauteng, Brigadier Mathapelo Peters.

Brigadier Peters: Two suspects were arrested within 24 hours of that incident. We believe that these people who are responsible for these killings were part of those groups that were marching on that day.

Macfarlane: Look a lot of them are saying they are doing this because there is a lack of policing.

Brigadier Peters: They were talking about a list of suspects who were known and when we checked with the police there were no previous criminal records nor were there any cases opened against them.

VO: Many people in the community are against the mob’s actions.

Sound up community person: Let us not kill each other, that’s not the solution.

Macfarlane: So did you see the people that did this to you?

Siyanda: There is one that I recognised. He is the one who was beating me the hardest and asking me “where are the people's genitals that you guys throw away at Yende?”

VO: Siyanda denied any knowledge of the mutilations saying he had left the gangs, but the mob was rabid. They believed they had found evidence pointing to gangs as perpetrators of the Yende park murders.

Nonkululeko: So apparently one of the gang members stole a jacket and a watch from one of the dead people, so that is how the community found out that these are the boys who are the ones who have been killing the people.

VO: When we asked the Brigadier about the body mutilations, she seemed to know only of one incident, even though the community report three.

Brigadier Peters: We are aware of one body that was found by a passerby, that case is with the police it is under investigation by one of our specialised units.

VO: But gangsters and vigilante mobs don’t seem to be the only perpetrators in Daveyton.

LINK: On the night that the Daveyton community went on the rampage, police, who were meant to restore calm, turned on ordinary civilians, two young girls, firing into their home.

VO: Nonkululeko and her cousin were standing outside their house when the police arrived.

Nonkululeko: Her kids were standing by the stoep she told them, "Let's go inside the house because the police are talking to us aggressively."

VO: Together with her daughters, Nonkululeko’s cousin walked towards the back of the house

Nonkululeko: I hear gunshots. This is the place where he placed his gun here, right here. My cousin saw this guy actually shooting. The next thing I hear my cousin's daughter screaming and saying, "Mom! I got shot!"

VO: The 15 year old girl had been hit by a spray of shotgun pellets.

Nonkululeko: I quickly went out and the police were already gone.

VO: Nonkululeko called for an ambulance. It arrived together with the Daveyton police.

Nonkululeko: The police that actually shot her, were Benoni Police. Their cars were written "Benoni Police". The Daveyton police they were even shocked. They were like, "He was not even supposed to use this kind of ammunition."

VO: The family opened a case of attempted murder against the Benoni police. It took five days to get a case number, and three weeks to reach the Independent Police Investigative Directorate. National spokesperson Moses Dlamini explains.

Moses Dlamini: The police are supposed to report any matter that falls within the mandate of the IPID within 24 hours// in writing, so they've already fallen foul but we must do an investigation first.

VO: The investigation will have to ascertain what kind of ammunition was used and why such force, if any, was necessary on innocent bystanders. // For now, the police have declared Daveyton a crime hot spot and community assistance programs are reportedly being implemented, but its residents are still uneasy

Nolwazi: It's that I fear for my child that maybe when he comes out of hospital he will be attacked again. Even at the hospital I'm not sure how safe he is.

Nonkululeko: Who should we trust, especially in this community? After the community is doing this. The mob is doing this. Now the police are doing this. Who are we supposed to turn to?

Siyanda: I got a chance to get into a container. I poured water over myself and it killed the fire. VO: But Siyanda was recaptured and dragged to Unity Secondary School. The mob went on a rampage looking for more gang members, even assaulting the headmaster. When they couldn’t find any they burned Siyanda outside the school grounds. Siyanda: They decided to use the tyre that was already burning and they threw me onto it. That's when I took it and threw it back and then one of them hit me with a stick on the head. I couldn't see clearly, I just heard the police arrive. That's when they ran away. VO: Since this violence, policing has been heightened in the area says SAPS Head of communication for Gauteng, Brigadier Mathapelo Peters. Brigadier Peters: Two suspects were arrested within 24 hours of that incident. We believe that these people who are responsible for these killings were part of those groups that were marching on that day. Macfarlane: Look a lot of them are saying they are doing this because there is a lack of policing. Brigadier Peters: They were talking about a list of suspects who were known and when we checked with the police there were no previous criminal records nor were there any cases opened against them. VO: Many people in the community are against the mob’s actions. Sound up community person: Let us not kill each other, that’s not the solution. Macfarlane: So did you see the people that did this to you? Siyanda: There is one that I recognised. He is the one who was beating me the hardest and asking me “where are the people's genitals that you guys throw away at Yende?” VO: Siyanda denied any knowledge of the mutilations saying he had left the gangs, but the mob was rabid. They believed they had found evidence pointing to gangs as perpetrators of the Yende park murders. Nonkululeko: So apparently one of the gang members stole a jacket and a watch from one of the dead people, so that is how the community found out that these are the boys who are the ones who have been killing the people. VO: When we asked the Brigadier about the body mutilations, she seemed to know only of one incident, even though the community report three. Brigadier Peters: We are aware of one body that was found by a passerby, that case is with the police it is under investigation by one of our specialised units. VO: But gangsters and vigilante mobs don’t seem to be the only perpetrators in Daveyton. LINK: On the night that the Daveyton community went on the rampage, police, who were meant to restore calm, turned on ordinary civilians, two young girls, firing into their home. VO: Nonkululeko and her cousin were standing outside their house when the police arrived. Nonkululeko: Her kids were standing by the stoep she told them, "Let's go inside the house because the police are talking to us aggressively." VO: Together with her daughters, Nonkululeko’s cousin walked towards the back of the house Nonkululeko: I hear gunshots. This is the place where he placed his gun here, right here. My cousin saw this guy actually shooting. The next thing I hear my cousin's daughter screaming and saying, "Mom! I got shot!" VO: The 15 year old girl had been hit by a spray of shotgun pellets. Nonkululeko: I quickly went out and the police were already gone. VO: Nonkululeko called for an ambulance. It arrived together with the Daveyton police. Nonkululeko: The police that actually shot her, were Benoni Police. Their cars were written "Benoni Police". The Daveyton police they were even shocked. They were like, "He was not even supposed to use this kind of ammunition." VO: The family opened a case of attempted murder against the Benoni police. It took five days to get a case number, and three weeks to reach the Independent Police Investigative Directorate. National spokesperson Moses Dlamini explains. Moses Dlamini: The police are supposed to report any matter that falls within the mandate of the IPID within 24 hours// in writing, so they've already fallen foul but we must do an investigation first. VO: The investigation will have to ascertain what kind of ammunition was used and why such force, if any, was necessary on innocent bystanders. // For now, the police have declared Daveyton a crime hot spot and community assistance programs are reportedly being implemented, but its residents are still uneasy Nolwazi: It's that I fear for my child that maybe when he comes out of hospital he will be attacked again. Even at the hospital I'm not sure how safe he is. Nonkululeko: Who should we trust, especially in this community? After the community is doing this. The mob is doing this. Now the police are doing this. Who are we supposed to turn to?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The community of Daveyton is under siege by Nyaope gangs. Fed up with the lack of policing in their township they took the law into their hands with dire consequences.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A lack of police response to violence perpetrated in the Daveyton community, in the east rand of Johannesburg, has prompted residents to take revenge against the gang members by using vigilante township justice, with tyres and matchsticks in defense of their own peace and safety. The feeling is that the police have failed them.
metadata.Summary: For some time now residents in Daveyton have been terrorized by thieves breaking into their homes. People are being killed in the streets by the gangs with little or no police intervention. In the past few weeks, violence escalated as the gangs went on a rampage. According Nonkululeko, a Daveyton resident, the gangs try and recruit young girls and boys and if they refuse they get necklaced. In the space of seven weeks 11 people have been killed. On the 15th of August things got out of control, following the murder of two teenage girls by the gangs. The community turned vigilante and went in search of gang members. They say that some of the gang members attend the local school, Unity Secondary school and it was there that they took justice into their own hands by necklacing alleged gang members in front of children and staff. These gruesome visuals have been shared on social media. Crime has always been an issue for the people of Daveyton, but with the emergence of gangs such as the “Freaks” and the “Avanzas” within the township the residents are afraid for their lives and those of their children and angry about a distinct lack of police protection. Finally, when they took matters into their own hands, the police reacted, patrolling the township trying to stop more bloodshed. This was only after the mob of residents necklaced the high school student suspected to be part of a gang. But the police themselves became perpetrators in the violence.
metadata.Further information: In the aftermath of the violence Gauteng MEC Panyaza Lesufi along with Gauteng Community Safety MEC Sizakele Nkosi-Malobane visited the Unity Secondary school and the community to plead for calm and patience. MEC Nkosi Malobane says they have a couple of arrests and more will follow. Lesufi believes schools are a place of learning and gangterism should not interrupt the children’s learning. According to Nonkululeko, while the police were patrolling the township, she and her cousin Petunia were standing outside their home when the police instructed them to go into the house. Nonkululeko says, she told them that they were not doing anything and were just standing there watching what was going on. When the police became aggressive, she and her cousin went into the house. While they were walking to the house one of the policemen put a rifle through the fence and shot at them three times with live ammunition. Petunia’s 15-year-old child was shot in the leg and as a result had to be sent to hospital. The cops that shot at them are believed to be from Benoni Police and when they called for assistance after the shooting it was Daveyton cops that arrived and told them to open a case against the Benoni police. Today, Pertunia’s child was sent back from hospital, with bullets still in her body and it’s alleged that the hospital told them the bullets will come out on their own. A couple of students who have also been approached by the gangs to join them have come forward to Carte Blanche as they continue to worry about their safety. Not only are children in the community traumatized by the gangs but the actions of the community has had them fearing to go to school. The residents of Daveyton live in fear and gangs are running rampant. Instead of the Police protecting them, there is more misery and brutality from the very same police. Cart Blanche investigates the turmoil.
